title: Pavarana
hookLine: at the rains' end monks invite each other to point out their faults

lines: IF YOU SAW ANYTHING, TELL ME.
cards: Imagine your workplace holds a meeting at the end of the year.

Everyone sits in a circle, and one by one, starting with the most senior, each says to the group: if you've seen me do anything wrong, or heard of it, or even suspected it, please tell me. Out of kindness, tell me.
Most offices would rather do anything else. Buddhist monks have done exactly this at the end of every rains retreat for over two thousand years. It's called Pavarana, the invitation.

teach.b: The Vinaya tells how it began. A group of monks spent a rains retreat together and, to avoid any quarrel, agreed not to speak to each other at all, all season.
They got through it peacefully and went to tell the Buddha. He did not praise them. Living together like that, in silence to avoid friction, isn't living at ease, he said.

At the end of the rains, each monk invites the community to speak to him about anything seen, heard or suspected. Out of compassion, speak to me, the invitation goes, and if I see the fault, I will make amends.
Each monk says it three times. Notice the three: seen, heard, suspected. Not just proven.
You're inviting the uncomfortable thing someone wasn't sure enough to say. The Connected Sayings tell how the Buddha himself did it.

At one Pavarana, sitting with five hundred monks, he invited them first: is there anything I have done, in body or in speech, that you would criticize? Sariputta answered for them: no, sir. The teacher went first.

In Thailand, Laos and Myanmar, this full moon also brings festivals of light, candles, lanterns and boats of light on rivers, and in some places the story that the Buddha came down from heaven this very day, which comes in two days.
But the core is a sentence: tell me my faults. It's a hard sentence, and a brave one, and it keeps a community honest.

how: At the end of the rains retreat, Theravada monks gather and each in turn formally invites the community to point out his faults; lay communities in Thailand, Laos and Myanmar mark the same full moon with merit-making and festivals of light.

s: the Buddha praised the monks who kept silent all season to avoid quarrels

games.q: you and your companions got through the rains retreat by never speaking. you tell the Buddha proudly. what does he say?
o: that's no way to live together; invite each other to speak.
games.why: he doesn't praise the silence. he sets the invitation: each monk asks the others to point out his faults, out of compassion.

practice: Bring to mind someone who knows you well and wishes you well, and imagine asking them: is there anything I do that you think I should see? Notice what happens in the body, tightness or heat, and breathe with it.
Then picture their answer arriving, and you taking it in calmly, with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Pavarana. The invitation at the end of the rains, when each monk asks the community to point out any fault seen, heard or suspected. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pavarana: invitation, the ceremony that ends the rains retreat.

carryVoice: Your line: tell me my faults. Asked out of kindness, heard with thanks. See you tomorrow.
